clips.text_en_b1: BTC does nothing for weeks and everyone ignores it. Then it pumps 15%, and suddenly everyone wants to buy in. Why does everyone want to buy after the move already happened? Classic retail behavior.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ rant about retail buying BTC after the move

signal.rationale: Post is rhetorical complaint about retail timing, no setup

clips.text_en_b2: BTC spent weeks drifting sideways and absolutely nobody gave a damn. Then it suddenly pumped fifteen percent and, predictably, every retail trader on the planet rushed back in, wallets open. Buying after the move has already happened is basically the textbook definition of catching a falling knife, yet this pattern repeats itself cycle after cycle. While seasoned investors were loading up quietly weeks ago, the herd shows up right when the easy gains are gone — pure human nature in action.
clips.text_en_c1: The market psychology on display whenever Bitcoin moves is, to seasoned observers, almost depressingly predictable. For weeks on end, the asset stagnates, generating barely a murmur from retail participants who profess to believe in its long-term thesis. The moment it rallies some fifteen percent, however, the same cohort materialises en masse, eager to establish positions at levels that any prudent trader would consider late entries. This phenomenon, often lampooned as buying the top after attempting to catch the bottom, speaks to a deeply ingrained behavioural tic. Were one to design a strategy guaranteed to underperform, it would look something like this. Human nature, it seems, remains remarkably consistent across cycles.
clips.text_en_c2: Bitcoin spent several interminable weeks drifting sideways in that peculiarly purgatorial state markets inhabit when nothing whatsoever is happening, and the retail cohort collectively lost interest with the predictability of seasonal migration. Then, as though on some preordained cue, it surged fifteen percent in short order — and the very same crowd that had yawned through the accumulation phase promptly stampeded back in, FOMO metastasising into action. The question remains perennial and, frankly, philosophically intriguing: why do retail participants, time and again, capitulate only after the move has materialised? Catching falling knives at the summit, mistaking vertigo for altitude — one ventures that this is not merely behavioural tic but a kind of involuntary reflex hardwired into the species, an atavistic impulse to chase momentum rather than anticipate it.

clips.text_en_b2: A thread on /g/ is debating which tech jobs might genuinely hold up against AI over the coming decades. Although white-collar automation tends to dominate the headlines, even supposedly safe fields like civil engineering and land surveying could be vulnerable as drones combined with AI increasingly handle point-cloud processing. The whole licensing pipeline takes years to complete, by which point the job market itself may have shifted beneath you. Pretty grim when even skilled trades aren't necessarily a safe bet for graduates.
clips.text_en_c1: A recurring thread on /g/ asks which technology-adjacent professions are likely to withstand the encroachment of artificial intelligence over the coming decades — a question that grows ever more pertinent as automation encroaches upon roles once considered untouchable. Even disciplines historically grounded in manual expertise, such as civil engineering and surveying, are scarcely immune; drone-captured imagery processed through AI-powered point-cloud software has already begun supplanting traditional site workflows, which renders years spent pursuing professional licensure a precarious investment at best. Whether any white-collar niche can plausibly claim genuine immunity remains, however, an open question that no amount of optimism can definitively resolve.
clips.text_en_c2: The /g/ thread poses what has rapidly become the defining occupational anxiety of our era: which technical specialisms, if any, can plausibly claim immunity from the relentless encroachment of artificial intelligence over the coming decades? The consensus appears to be that virtually no white-collar discipline remains sacrosanct — even civil engineering and land surveying, traditionally bastions of human-only labour, are undergoing quiet but inexorable automation as drones coupled with machine-vision algorithms render point-cloud generation and site reconnaissance increasingly autonomous. The poster himself, still ensconced in the purgatory of professional licensure, concedes that his own trajectory depends upon AI tools keeping him gainfully employed — a confession that is either pragmatic or damning, depending on one's temperament. The unspoken corollary, of course, is that genuine AI-proof roles may prove vanishingly scarce.

While the thread itself is obvious shitpost material, the underlying concern is legitimate enough — rare-earth supply chains remain a genuine choke point for EV manufacturing, missile guidance systems, and a wide range of defence applications. The Global Times certainly wouldn't run with that particular framing, but the strategic vulnerability is real.
clips.text_en_c1: The discourse on /pol/ today has descended into its customary territory of geopolitical fantasy, wherein China's rare-earth magnet technology is characterised as quasi-alien in origin and the thread collectively demands that Beijing transfer the relevant know-how to Washington 'or else.' While the proposition is, naturally, satirical to its core, the underlying anxiety it masks is anything but fictional: rare-earth supply chains constitute a genuine chokepoint for industries ranging from electric vehicle manufacturing to precision-guided munitions. Should Beijing ever choose to weaponise that dependency, the consequences would extend far beyond the realm of shitposting.
clips.text_en_c2: The /pol/ board has, with admirable predictability, descended into another breathless episode of strategic illiteracy: Chinese magnet manufacturing capabilities are being characterised as quasi-alien technology, and the thread demands — with the diplomatic subtlety one has come to expect from that particular forum — that Beijing immediately transfer these processes to the United States, or else suffer consequences presumably too fearsome to articulate. It is the sort of geopolitical analysis one would expect from a comment section populated entirely by people who have never read a single supply-chain white paper. And yet, beneath the irredeemable shitpost veneer, the underlying observation is not entirely without merit: rare-earth element supply chains constitute a genuine chokepoint for EV manufacture, wind turbine production, and the precision guidance systems underpinning modern missile programmes.

clips.text_en_c2: The original poster, who had evidently taken a fitness influencer's cut advice as gospel, now finds himself in the grimly ironic predicament of having shed a staggering forty-five pounds over a mere twelve weeks only to discover that his gym performance has correspondingly evaporated.
